Welcome to my website! I am a Ph.D. candidate in Finance at the University of Piraeus. My research lies at the
intersection of empirical asset pricing, sustainable finance, option-implied expected returns, and textual analysis,
with a particular focus on how corporate labor misconduct is reflected in financial markets.

I have worked as a Research Assistant at the <a href="https://www.kep.unipi.gr" target="_blank">
University of Piraeus Research Centre </a> and I am also an <a href="https://iffr.gr/" target="_blank">
IFFR Doctoral Fellow </a>. Prior to my doctoral studies, I gained industry experience in consulting and shipping,
working at <a href="https://www.pwc.com/" target="_blank">PwC</a>, TMS Bunkers, and Seacharm Navigation.

I will be on the 2026-27 academic job market. Please feel free to reach out if you would like to discuss my research or
potential collaborations.





<h3>Working Papers</h3>




<hr>
<section class="paper">
<p class="mb-1">
<a class="paper-title"
   href="working_papers/Corporate Labor Misconduct Risk 20260729.pdf">
Corporate Labor Misconduct Risk: Evidence from 10-K Disclosures and Enforcement
</a>
(with
<a href="https://sites.google.com/view/george-skiadopoulos"
   target="_blank"
   rel="noopener noreferrer">
George Skiadopoulos
</a>).<br>
<a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6780582">
July 2026 Draft
</a>
<a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6780582">
[SSRN]
</a>
<br>
<strong><em><u>Job Market Paper</u></em></strong>
</p>
<details class="mt-1">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<p>
Despite growing attention to corporate misconduct, firm-level measures of corporate labor misconduct risk remain limited.
We develop novel textual measures of labor misconduct risk for U.S.-listed firms by combining 10-K risk disclosures with
labor-related violation and penalty data and a comprehensive labor-risk dictionary. The measures capture distinct
dimensions of labor misconduct related to benefit and wage violations, employment discrimination, and workplace safety.
They predict subsequent enforcement actions, exhibit patterns consistent with regulatory and industry variation, and are
associated with future stock return volatility. While realized stock returns show no significant labor risk premium,
option-implied expected returns reveal a strong size pattern: the premium is positive for large firms but negative for
small firms. The differential pricing of labor misconduct risk across firm size is consistent with differences in firms'
information environments.
</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Presented at:</strong>
<a href="https://www.fmarc.eu" target="_blank">FMARC</a>, Ayia Napa June 30, 2026,
<a href="https://www.fma.org" target="_blank">FMA European Conference</a>, Braga June 12, 2026,
<a href="https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/jrc-summer-school-sustainable-finance/jrc-summer-school-sustainable-finance-7th-edition-2025-07-10_en" target="_blank">7th JRC Summer School on Sustainable Finance</a>, Ispra July 10, 2025,
and <a href="https://www.therisksociety.com" target="_blank">IRMC</a>, Bari June 24, 2025.

</li>
</ul>
</details>
</section>







<section class="paper">
<p class="mb-1">
<span class="nodraftpaper">
Market Risk Premium: What do Option Markets Tell Us?
</span>
(with
<a href="https://sites.google.com/view/george-skiadopoulos"
   target="_blank"
   rel="noopener noreferrer">
George Skiadopoulos
</a>).
</p>
<details class="mt-1">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<p>
Prior research documents that option-implied information outperforms historical returns in estimating the market
risk premium for market-timing strategies in the U.S. up to 2010. We revisit this evidence using a longer sample
that includes major global shocks, a multi-country setting (U.S., U.K., Germany, Japan, and South Korea), and
alternative methods for extracting information from option prices. Our findings indicate that option-implied measures
still outperform historical ones, but mainly for less risk-averse investors and when model parameters are estimated
with recent data. These results are robust across multiple evaluation metrics and historical benchmarks, though the
best-performing option-based method varies across time periods, reflecting differing dynamics in option-implied risk
premia.
</p>
<ul>
</ul>
</details>
</section>





<section class="paper">
<p class="mb-1">
<span class="nodraftpaper">
Are Corporate Labor Misconduct Risks Priced in the Cross-Section of US Bond Returns?
</span>
(with
<a href="https://sites.google.com/view/george-skiadopoulos"
   target="_blank"
   rel="noopener noreferrer">
George Skiadopoulos
</a>).
</p>
<details class="mt-1">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<p>
We examine whether various dimensions of corporate labor misconduct risk is priced in the cross-section of U.S.
corporate bond returns over 2007–2024. We employ Politis and Skiadopoulos, 2026, textual firm-level measures of
corporate labor misconduct risk and transaction-based bond returns from Enhanced TRACE. Univariate portfolio sorts and
bond-level cross-sectional regressions yield no evidence for labor risks to be priced. On the other hand, bivariate
portfolio sorts identify that risks stemming from employment discrimination are priced among financially constrained,
small with greater probability to default firms. However, the evidence vanishes when portfolios are formed within
industries, while workplace safety risk turn out to be priced among financially constrained issuers. Our findings
indicate that investors assess labor risks differently relative to the operating conditions of each industry. Overall,
the evidence provides limited support for a pervasive labor risk premium, but suggests a workplace safety premium among
financially constrained issuers.
</p>
<ul>
</ul>
</details>
</section>
